entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5146"/><div sID="gen7657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5146"/>24-25. Job asserts his freedom from trust in money (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>). Here he turns to his duty towards God, as before he had spoken of his duty towards himself and his neighbor. Covetousness is covert idolatry, as it transfers the heart from the Creator to the creature (<reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.27">27</reference> he passes to overt idolatry. <div eID="gen7657" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5147"/><div sID="gen7658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5147"/>26. If I looked unto the sun (as an object of worship) because he shined; or to the moon because she walked, &c. Sabaism (from tsaba, "the heavenly hosts") was the earliest form of false worship. God is hence called in contradistinction, "Lord of Sabaoth." The sun, moon, and stars, the brightest objects in nature, and seen everywhere, were supposed to be visible representatives of the invisible God. They had no temples, but were worshipped on high places and roofs of houses (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">De 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">11</reference>). The Hebrew here for "sun" is light. Probably light was worshipped as the emanation from God, before its embodiments, the sun, &c. This worship prevailed in Chaldea; wherefore Job's exemption from the idolatry of his neighbors was the more exemplary. Our "Sun-day," "Mon-day," or Moon-day, bear traces of Sabaism. <div eID="gen7658" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5152"/><div sID="gen7665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5152"/>31. That is, Job's household said, Oh, that we had Job's enemy to devour, we cannot rest satisfied till we have! But Job refrained from even wishing revenge (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8">1Sa 26:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">2Sa 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">10</reference>). So Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.54">Lu 9:54</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">55</reference>). But, better (see <reference osisRef="Job.31.32">Job 31:32</reference>), translated, "Who can show (literally, give) the man who was not satisfied with the flesh (meat) provided by Job?" He never let a poor man leave his gate without giving him enough to eat. <div eID="gen7665" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5154"/><div sID="gen7667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5154"/><hi type="bold">33. Adam--</hi>translated by Umbreit, "as men do" (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.7">Ho 6:7</reference>, where see Margin). But English Version is more natural. The very same word for "hiding" is used in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.8">Ge 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.10">10</reference>, of Adam hiding himself from God. Job elsewhere alludes to the flood. So he might easily know of the fall, through the two links which connect Adam and Abraham (about Job's time), namely, Methuselah and Shem. Adam is representative of fallen man's propensity to concealment (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Pr 28:13</reference>). It was from God that Job did not "hide his iniquity in his bosom," as on the contrary it was from God that "Adam" hid in his lurking-place. This disproves the translation, "as men"; for it is from their fellow men that "men" are chiefly anxious to hide their real character as guilty. Magee, to make the comparison with Adam more exact, for my "bosom" translates, "lurking-place." <div eID="gen7667" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5155"/><div sID="gen7668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5155"/><hi type="bold">34. Rather, the apodosis to <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>, "Then let me be fear-stricken before a great multitude, let the contempt, &c., let me keep silence (the greatest disgrace to a patriot, heretofore so prominent in assemblies), and not go out," &c. A just retribution that he who hides his sin from God, should have it exposed before man (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.12">2Sa 12:12</reference>). But Job had not been so exposed, but on the contrary was esteemed in the assemblies of the "tribes"--</hi>("families"); a proof, he implies, that God does not hold him guilty of hiding sin (<reference osisRef="Job.24.16">Job 24:16</reference>, contrast with <reference osisRef="Job.29.21-Job.29.25">Job 29:21-25</reference>). <div eID="gen7668" type="x-p"/>

But Job had not been so exposed, but on the contrary was esteemed in the assemblies of the "tribes"-- ("families"); a proof, he implies, that God does not hold him guilty of hiding sin ( Job 24:16 , contrast with Job 29:21-25 ).

Job returns to his wish (<reference osisRef="Job.13.22">Job 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">19:23</reference>). Omit "is"; "Behold my sign," that is, my mark of subscription to the statements just given in my defense: the mark of signature was originally a cross; and hence the letter Tau or T. Translate, also "Oh, that the Almighty," &c. He marks "God" as the "One" meant in the first clause.<div eID="gen7669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adversary--</hi>that is, he who contends with me, refers also to God. entries.content_plain: 35. Job returns to his wish ( Job 13:22 ; 19:23 ). Omit "is"; "Behold my sign," that is, my mark of subscription to the statements just given in my defense: the mark of signature was originally a cross; and hence the letter Tau or T. Translate, also "Oh, that the Almighty," &c. He marks "God" as the "One" meant in the first clause. adversary-- that is, he who contends with me, refers also to God. The vagueness is designed to express "whoever it be that judicially opposes me"--the Almighty if it be He. had written a book-- rather, "would write down his charge."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5159"/><div sID="gen7676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5159"/>38. Personification. The complaints of the unjustly ousted proprietors are transferred to the lands themselves (<reference osisRef="Job.31.20">Job 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Ge 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">Ha 2:11</reference>). If I have unjustly acquired lands (<reference osisRef="Job.24.2">Job 24:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Is 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen7676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furrows--</hi>The specification of these makes it likely, he implies in this, "If I paid not the laborer for tillage"; as <reference osisRef="Job.31.39">Job 31:39</reference>, "If I paid him not for gathering in the fruits." Thus of the four clauses in <reference osisRef="Job.31.38">Job 31:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.39">39</reference>, the first refers to the same subject as the fourth, the second is connected with the third by introverted parallelism. Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jas 5:4</reference>, which plainly alludes to this passage: compare "Lord of Sabaoth" with <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference> here. <div eID="gen7677" type="x-p"/>

But <reference osisRef="Job.31.38-Job.31.40">Job 31:38-40</reference> are naturally added by one whose mind in agitation recurs to its sense of innocence, even after it has come to the usual stopping point; this takes away the appearance of rhetorical artifice. entries.content_plain: 40. thistles-- or brambles, thorns. cockle-- literally, "noxious weeds." The words ... ended-- that is, in the controversy with the friends. He spoke in the book afterwards, but not to them. At Job 31:37 would be the regular conclusion in strict art. But Job 31:38-40 are naturally added by one whose mind in agitation recurs to its sense of innocence, even after it has come to the usual stopping point; this takes away the appearance of rhetorical artifice. Hence the transposition by Eichorn of Job 31:38-40 to follow Job 31:25 is quite unwarranted.
